  relationship_status: Divorced

  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Auditory (Babies): Babies
  Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere

Vignette:
Layla traces the grout lines on the floor with her eyes, a familiar way to anchor herself when the room feels like it’s tilting. At thirty-four, she feels ancient. It has been eight months since the day the world cracked open. Before that day, life was about the rhythm of the seasons, the ache in her back from working the fields, the small comforts of a shared meal. She worked alongside the same families year after year, a community bound by sun and soil. She knew their stories, their struggles. She thought she knew them. That was her first mistake. The day it happened was hot and still. During a lunch break, she was sitting near the trailer of a family she was fond of, a young couple with a new baby. She could hear their voices through the thin wall, tense and sharp, something about money owed. Layla tried not to listen, focusing on her food, but then she saw the husband, Amir, step outside. He paced back and forth, rubbing the back of his neck, his eyes scanning the horizon as if looking for an enemy. She registered it as odd, a flicker of unease, but dismissed it. An hour later, the screaming started. It wasn't just the baby's wail, a sound she now understands as a prelude to horror, but the wife's. Layla saw Amir, the man who had shared jokes with her that morning, his face a mask of rage she had never imagined. The memory isn't a story she can tell; it’s a series of frozen images and sounds that crash into her without warning.

The world that reassembled itself afterward was a different, more dangerous place. At her new job on a different farm, she cannot bear to be near coworkers when they argue, even playfully. If a conversation turns to finances or family trouble, a cold dread seeps into her limbs and she has to walk away, pretending she needs to check on the irrigation lines. She watches everyone now, especially the men. A gesture of frustration, a tense jaw, a colleague looking around too quickly—these are not just moods, but omens. She has come to believe that a placid surface hides unknowable violence, that people are not what they seem, and it is her job to find the threat before it finds her. The sound of a baby crying is the worst. In the supermarket last month, a tired infant began to wail in the next aisle, and Layla dropped her basket, milk and eggs smashing on the floor, as she fled to her car, her heart hammering against her ribs as if trying to escape her body.

Her life has shrunk to the four walls of her small apartment. Her husband left three months ago, tired of what he called her ghosts. He couldn’t understand why she would flinch from his touch, or why she spent every evening scrubbing the floors and countertops until her hands were raw. But for Layla, the ritual of cleaning is the only thing that makes sense. If she can impose perfect order on her home, she feels she can keep the chaos of the world from breaching her door. It is a fragile defense. When the intrusive images come—of Amir’s face, of his wife’s eyes—she tries to violently shove them from her mind, turning up the radio until it’s just noise, or forcing herself to think of something, anything, positive. *It’s a beautiful day. The sky is blue. I am safe here.* The words are hollow, a desperate mantra she repeats against a tide of terror. She feels utterly alone, a foreigner not in her country but in her own life. The faith she once had in people, in a just world, has evaporated, leaving behind a hard, bitter certainty that she belongs nowhere and can trust no one. She came to therapy after her supervisor found her hyperventilating behind a packing shed, triggered by two workers having a heated discussion. What frightens her most is the conviction that this vigilance is the only thing keeping her alive. What she hopes for, in a voice so quiet she can barely hear it herself, is to one day stand in the sun and not be searching for a shadow.
